chunks: "A flip chip is a die that is mounted upside down.

Instead of gluing the die face-up and connecting thin wires from the edge pads to the package, you put a solder bump or copper pillar on each pad, flip the die over so the active side faces the substrate, and reflow it so the bumps make the connection directly.
Then you fill the gap with underfill epoxy. Compared to wire bonding there are big advantages.
The connection is tens of micrometres long rather than millimetres, so inductance drops from nanohenries to tens of picohenries, which is great for high-speed I/O and for power delivery.
The bumps can be spread over the whole die as an array, so you can have thousands of connections instead of being limited to the perimeter, and you can feed power straight to the middle of the die.
And the back of the die is free, so a heat spreader or heat sink can touch it directly. The downsides are cost and mechanics.
You need bumping on the wafer, a fine-pitch substrate, and underfill.
Silicon and an organic substrate expand differently, so the bumps see shear stress when the temperature changes, which is why underfill is needed.
You can't see the joints without X-ray, and rework is hard.
So it's used for CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs and anything high-pin-count or high-current, while cheap, low-pin-count parts stay wire-bonded."
